input.rationale: Closing the plateau question from source rather than another execution. The in-memory snapshot store creates each snapshot by replacing its single latest entry and its List returns exactly that one snapshot, so a stored-snapshot count is not a count of snapshot attempts for that store; the file-backed store used by the default cluster helper similarly reaps older snapshots according to its retain count. The observed sequence 1 then 2 then 3 and then flat is therefore consistent with attempts continuing while what the store reports stops tracking them, and my earlier reading of that count as an attempt counter was unsound. This does not change the defect: the spurious verdict and the redundant snapshot creation are still witnessed, but the consequence statement must be phrased in terms of attempts at an unchanged index, and any future cadence measurement must count attempts (for example by observing the FSM's Snapshot calls or the store's Create calls) instead of stored snapshots.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose applied index already equals its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. Parsed index 0 of CheckRun a4a0cbfa094b4d1982032d9de0652861 contradicts it (store_last=0 against snapshot_index=3 with applied_index=3 and should_snapshot=true) and the verdict held through every later sample of that run, so the spurious trigger is established independently of any timing question. The consequence is witnessed as snapshot creation at the unchanged index while the applied index stayed at 3: the stored count moved 1 to 2 to 3 across parsed indices 1 and 2, which requires at least two successful creations. Reading the in-memory snapshot store shows why that count then flattened: Create replaces the single latest snapshot and List returns only that one, so the stored count cannot be used as an attempt counter, and the file-backed store used by the cluster helper reaps older snapshots per its retain count. The flat tail therefore does not show that the loop stopped; it shows my proxy stopped measuring, and I withdraw both the per-interval wording and any inference from the flat tail. The claim stands on the persistent spurious verdict plus the redundant creation actually witnessed, with cadence left unmeasured.
limitations: Cadence remains unmeasured: stored-snapshot counts cannot serve as an attempt counter for these stores, so any rate claim needs an attempt-level observation such as the FSM's Snapshot calls.

The claim is bounded to the spurious verdict and redundant snapshot creation at an unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety effect.

The wrapped store_last=18446744073709551615 from parsed index 1 onward comes from the in-memory log store's delete-range bookkeeping after repeated compaction and should not be attributed to other log stores; the generic reading is the emptied-store sample in parsed index 0.
The interval was set to 100ms for observation, far shorter than any production default, so observed timing is not a production cadence.
Single node, one process, in-process transports and an in-memory snapshot store, so the real cost of the redundant snapshots is understated.

interpretations.rationale: Source reading establishes the mechanism: the leader updates its own latest configuration and the commitment voter set at append time, and commitment is recomputed over the new voter set, so AddVoter success only means a quorum of the new configuration stored the entry. In an isolated native run of the submitted scenario the new configuration was already reported by all three nodes at the first sample (~1ms), i.e. no lasting disagreement. The earlier 'peer mismatch' occurred once during a full package run and did not reappear on a repeat run of the same suite. No source path was found that would keep a pre-existing voter's latest configuration permanently missing a committed configuration entry; the conflicting observation is currently attributed to harness timing under load, but that attribution is not yet grounded in a controller receipt.

Source reading already showed that the leader updates its own latest configuration and the commitment voter set at append time, so AddVoter success certifies only that a quorum of the new configuration stored the entry; combined with the follower-side behavior that latest configuration is set at log-store time, a pre-existing voter's reported configuration may legitimately lag the leader's by one replication delivery. The retained execution witnesses exactly that: the AddVoter future returned success at 2ms (index 1, err <nil>, index 3), the pre-existing voter server-d6f82acc reported num_servers=2/has_new_member=false at the same 2ms sample (index 3), and at 102ms the same server reported num_servers=3/has_new_member=true (index 6). All probes 6 through 91 (out to 2927ms) show 3 servers on that server, so the disagreement did not persist or recur within the observed window. The earlier unexplained 'peer mismatch' under full-suite load is thus consistent with the same bounded replication transient rather than a broken configuration-update path on pre-existing voters.
limitations: Single execution with two 100ms-spaced samples bracketing the transition: the exact instant the follower adopted the new configuration is only bounded to the interval (2ms, 102ms], so the observation shows boundedness, not a latency bound under load.
The sampled predicate is each node's locally reported latest configuration (getLatestConfiguration), not commit ordering; the samples say nothing about when the follower committed the entry.

The originally observed full-suite 'peer mismatch' lasted up to the harness 5s limit and was not reproduced in isolation, so its cause under CPU contention remains unmeasured; only its identity with this bounded transient is supported, not its duration.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account of the commit-eligibility rule. The three places that could let non-voter support count are all closed: the match set is built from Voter entries only at leader setup and at configuration change; match() rejects any server ID absent from that map, so a Nonvoter's AppendEntries response cannot create an entry; and recalculate derives commitIndex solely from the surviving map values. Replication is nonetheless started for every configured server, which explains why non-voters receive and store logs without ever contributing to commitment. No contradiction was found in the enclosing paths: the leader lease and election quorum helpers count the same Voter set, and processLogs is bounded by the leader's commitIndex. This is a source-explained negative, so no defect is asserted and the corresponding discriminator is left for execution rather than being inferred from the reading.
limitations: Source-only account: no retained execution yet exercises a mixed Voter/Nonvoter configuration, so the claim rests on reading the producers, not on an observed endpoint.
The reading covers the leader-side commit rule; it does not evaluate non-voter participation in any other mechanism (for example snapshot install or leadership transfer targeting a non-voter).

interpretations.rationale: Comparison: does commit progress track Voter acknowledgements only? Parsed index 2 is the withheld-Nonvoter case: the apply future completed with a nil error, leader_commit went from 3 to 4 and leader_last_index reached 4, while the Nonvoter's own last log index stayed 3, i.e. the entry committed although the Nonvoter never stored it, so nonvoter participation is not needed for commitment. Parsed index 3 is the withheld-Voter case: leader_last_before=4, the leader stored index 5, the Nonvoter stored index 5 as well (nonvoter_has_entry=true), and leader_commit still read 4 when sampled, while the apply future returned 'leadership lost while committing log' rather than success. Read together with the source-derived rule (match set contains only Voter IDs, match() ignores other IDs, recalculate reads only that set), the operands show a stored-and-acknowledged nonvoter entry that did not advance commitIndex. The apply error in case B comes from an independent mechanism - the leader could not contact a quorum of Voters within LeaderLeaseTimeout and stepped down - so case B does not isolate the commit rule by itself; the decisive evidence is the operand contrast between the Nonvoter's stored index and the unchanged commit index, and case A supplies the converse control in the same execution.
limitations: Case B's apply outcome is dominated by lease-driven leadership loss because a single-Voter failure already removes the Voter quorum in a two-Voter cluster, so that case does not alone separate 'commit rule ignores nonvoters' from 'leader stopped being leader'.

Sampling shows commitment had not advanced when polled immediately after the 800ms window; it does not rule out a later advance under a different schedule, though the fact itself is that the nonvoter's stored entry did not by itself advance commitIndex.
Single execution of each case in one process with in-process transports; the withheld-Server scenario assumes a clean transport-level isolation and does not model partial or asymmetric failure.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account of the restart/vote relationship. On startup the node restores currentTerm from the CurrentTerm stable key and the last log entry through setCurrentTerm/setLastLog, and nothing else vote-related is restored, so any same-term duplicate decision must come from the durable keys. In the vote handler the duplicate check reads LastVoteTerm and LastVoteCand from StableStore, returns granted only when the stored candidate bytes equal the requesting candidate, and otherwise returns without setting Granted, so a second different candidate in the same term is denied regardless of restart. persistVote writes the term first and then the candidate before the handler sets Granted, so an acknowledged vote is durable before the response. The older-term rejection is the earlier term comparison, and the restored currentTerm is what makes it effective after a restart. This is a source-explained negative - a protection that defeats an obvious candidate defect - so no defect is asserted and the discriminator is left for execution rather than inferred from reading.
limitations: Source-only: the restart behaviour is read from the constructors and handlers, not yet observed; in particular the claim that a new Raft instance does not consult any other persisted vote artefact rests on reading NewRaft and restoreSnapshot.
The account covers the vote path only; it does not evaluate whether a restart can otherwise reuse stale term or log state in a way that breaks safety (for example a truncated log tail).

interpretations.rationale: Declared predicate: after a restart, a same-term request for the already-voted candidate is still granted while the same-term request for a different candidate is denied, and an older-term request is denied. Parsed index 0 establishes the antecedent producer edge: a real RequestVote granted to candidate A in term 6 left the durable keys at LastVoteTerm=6 and LastVoteCand=A, and the node's term was 6. Parsed index 1 shows the durable vote survived the restart (restored_vote_term=7 with the same candidate A, restored currentTerm 7), but at a term the harness did not choose, because the subject stayed a live member of a real cluster and its peers advanced it past the probe term. Since the restored currentTerm exceeded every post-restart probe term, parsed index 2's three denials are explained by the older-term rule alone: the same-term branch (stored term equal to request term) was never reached, so the comparison's antecedent is unobserved and the predicate is unknown rather than satisfied or violated. The restart-persistence part of the source account is consistent with indices 0 and 1; the same-term-survival part is not yet decided.
limitations: The subject was not isolated: it remained an active voter whose real peers could advance its term, so the post-restart probes were not applicable to the same-term rule and the unknown outcome is a design limitation of this execution, not evidence about the code.

The pre-restart observation shows a grant and the durable keys, but the durable keys were overwritten by the cluster's own later vote at term 7 before the restart, so indices 0 and 1 do not by themselves isolate which request produced the persisted state.

Successor discriminator: isolate the target's transport from its peers (or use a configuration whose other voters are unreachable) before the restart probes, verify the restored currentTerm equals the probe term, and only then compare the same-candidate, other-candidate and older-term grants.

interpretations.rationale: Declared predicate: after a restart, a same-term request for the already-voted candidate is still granted, a same-term request for a different candidate is denied, and an older-term request is denied. Applicability is explicit in the receipt: parsed index 1 reports applicable=true with restored_term=6 and restored_vote_term=6, so the restored currentTerm equals the probe term and the same-term branch is reachable; parsed index 2 reports applicable=true and term_at_probe_end=6, so no election interposed during the probes and all three requests were delivered. Against that base, parsed index 2's operands are: same_cand_granted=true, other_cand_granted=false, older_term_granted=false. The one-candidate-per-term rule is thus preserved across a restart and is read from durable state, consistent with the source account that the handler loads LastVoteTerm/LastVoteCand on every request and that persistVote writes before the grant. This is a protective mechanism, so the account is a refuted suspicion rather than a defect.
limitations: One execution in one process with in-process transports and a rebuilt Raft over the same stores; it does not model a crash before the durable candidate key is written, and the write order (term then candidate) is taken from source rather than exercised.
The isolation used to keep the probe term applicable removes concurrent cluster activity, so the run does not evaluate the same-term branch while other real elections are in flight.
The probes exercise the vote handler through a dedicated transport; they do not exercise a full campaign where the candidate itself counts its own vote.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account. shouldSnapshot reads the log store's LastIndex and the cached last snapshot index and returns delta >= SnapshotThreshold, with delta computed as an unsigned subtraction. compactLogsWithTrailing deletes everything up to min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailingLogs), and both the snapshot-install path and the user-restore path set the snapshot index to at least the installed index while the log store keeps only newer entries; on a log store that tolerates gaps this can leave LastIndex below the snapshot index, so the subtraction underflows instead of being negative. The account therefore predicts a spurious positive verdict rather than a missed snapshot. I am not asserting a defect: the consequence I can source is limited to an extra snapshot attempt at an unchanged index, and whether that matters depends on consumer expectations for SnapshotThreshold that this snapshot does not settle.
limitations: Source-only: the underflow is derived from reading the arithmetic and the compaction callers, not observed; no retained execution yet shows the emptied-store state.
The consequence is bounded to snapshot scheduling; nothing in this reading shows loss of committed entries or a change to which entries are applied, so it should not be read as a safety claim.

The reachable variant depends on which SnapshotStore and LogStore are in use (monotonic stores remove all logs, gap-tolerant stores compact up to the snapshot), and neither variant has been exercised here.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose committed and applied index already equal its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. Parsed index 0 establishes the control verdict (store_last=4, snapshot_index=0, should_snapshot=false), so the threshold test is discriminating and the large SnapshotThreshold is not saturating the result. Parsed index 1 is the witness: after the production snapshot path ran (Snapshot -> runSnapshots -> takeSnapshot -> compactLogs) the log store was emptied (store_last=0) while the snapshot index was 4 and commit/applied stayed 4, yet shouldSnapshot returned true. Since shouldSnapshot computes delta as an unsigned difference between the store's last index and the snapshot index, the emptied store makes delta underflow rather than go negative, so the verdict becomes true with no new entry. The consequence follows from the same mechanism: runSnapshots calls takeSnapshot whenever shouldSnapshot holds, and takeSnapshot only refuses when the FSM has applied nothing at all, so the node re-creates a snapshot at an unchanged index at each SnapshotInterval. The witness is generated by the target's own compaction after a normal user snapshot, not by stubbing state.
limitations: Scope: the repeating effect requires the FSM's Snapshot to keep succeeding; if Snapshot/Persist errors, the loop reports the error instead and no snapshot is created.

The consequence observed and claimed is limited to redundant snapshot creation and its IO at an unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety violation, and the same index is snapshotted rather than a stale one.

Reached deterministically with TrailingLogs=0 so that compaction trims up to the snapshot index; the install-snapshot and monotonic-store variants that the source reading predicts were not exercised, so the frequency of the state in other configurations is not established.
Single node, one process, in-process transport and InmemStore; the snapshot store is in-memory, so the cost of the redundant snapshots is understated.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only extension. restoreUserSnapshot chooses a last index above both the snapshot and the current log, writes it as the last log and last applied, sets the snapshot to the same index, and then calls removeOldLogs when the log store reports monotonic; removeOldLogs compacts with a trailing count of zero, so a monotonic store ends with no entries while the cached snapshot index is the restored index. shouldSnapshot then compares the store's last index against the snapshot index with unsigned arithmetic, which underflows for that state. This predicts the same verdict as the retained witness but with default TrailingLogs, and it is a distinct producer (restore plus monotonic store) rather than compaction after a caller-configured snapshot. No defect judgment is added here: the existing assertion covers the mechanism, and this question settles only how widely the state is reachable.
limitations: Source-only: the restore-plus-monotonic-store state has not been observed; the claim that a monotonic store ends with an empty log rests on reading removeOldLogs and the caller's compaction contract.

The user-restore path is documented as a disaster-recovery operation that should not be used in normal operation, so reachability through it is a weaker practical case than compaction after an ordinary snapshot.

This question does not re-open the asserted defect or its bounded consequence; it only extends the set of producers, and a negative result would narrow the defect's reachability without changing the mechanism already witnessed.

interpretations.rationale: Promotion of the mechanism witnessed by the retained receipt into durable knowledge, so later interpretations can reuse it without re-reading snapshot.go. The arithmetic and the witness agree: the verdict flips to true in exactly the state where the store's last index is below the cached snapshot index, and the control in the same execution shows the verdict is false when the store still holds entries. Predicate: after a user restore on a monotonic log store with default snapshot configuration, the store's last index falls below the snapshot index and shouldSnapshot therefore reports true, repeating at each SnapshotInterval. Parsed index 1 contradicts it: store_last=105 against snapshot_index=104 with applied index 105 and restore_err nil, so store_emptied is false and should_snapshot is false; parsed index 2 confirms the verdict stays false after several intervals and the snapshot count does not grow. The mechanism that defeats the premise is visible in the sources: removeOldLogs does clear the log store during the restore, but the Restore API then appends a trailng noop entry and waits for it, which puts one log entry above the snapshot index and leaves a small positive delta instead of an underflow. Because the hypothesis is contradicted by the witness, the comparison is violated and this particular producer is refuted; the previously asserted defect stands on its own witness and is not weakened or extended by this result.
limitations: Single execution, one process, in-process transport, in-memory snapshot store and default TrailingLogs/SnapshotThreshold; the restored index was burned 100 above the log, and a restore whose index leaves a different residue was not tried.

The refutation covers the producer reached through Restore() on a monotonic store; it does not speak to the snapshot-install path on a follower, which the source reading also predicts and which remains unexercised.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate for this construction: a fresh node that receives an InstallSnapshot ends with its log store below its snapshot index, so shouldSnapshot reports true. interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose applied and commit indices already equal its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. The earlier 'peer mismatch' occurred once during a full package run and did not reappear on a repeat run of the same suite. No source path was found that would keep a pre-existing voter's latest configuration permanently missing a committed configuration entry; the conflicting observation is currently attributed to harness timing under load, but that attribution is not yet grounded in a controller receipt.

Source reading already showed that the leader updates its own latest configuration and the commitment voter set at append time, so AddVoter success certifies only that a quorum of the new configuration stored the entry; combined with the follower-side behavior that latest configuration is set at log-store time, a pre-existing voter's reported configuration may legitimately lag the leader's by one replication delivery. The retained execution witnesses exactly that: the AddVoter future returned success at 2ms (index 1, err <nil>, index 3), the pre-existing voter server-d6f82acc reported num_servers=2/has_new_member=false at the same 2ms sample (index 3), and at 102ms the same server reported num_servers=3/has_new_member=true (index 6). All probes 6 through 91 (out to 2927ms) show 3 servers on that server, so the disagreement did not persist or recur within the observed window. The earlier unexplained 'peer mismatch' under full-suite load is thus consistent with the same bounded replication transient rather than a broken configuration-update path on pre-existing voters.
limitations: Single execution with two 100ms-spaced samples bracketing the transition: the exact instant the follower adopted the new configuration is only bounded to the interval (2ms, 102ms], so the observation shows boundedness, not a latency bound under load.
The sampled predicate is each node's locally reported latest configuration (getLatestConfiguration), not commit ordering; the samples say nothing about when the follower committed the entry.

The originally observed full-suite 'peer mismatch' lasted up to the harness 5s limit and was not reproduced in isolation, so its cause under CPU contention remains unmeasured; only its identity with this bounded transient is supported, not its duration.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account of the commit-eligibility rule. The three places that could let non-voter support count are all closed: the match set is built from Voter entries only at leader setup and at configuration change; match() rejects any server ID absent from that map, so a Nonvoter's AppendEntries response cannot create an entry; and recalculate derives commitIndex solely from the surviving map values. Replication is nonetheless started for every configured server, which explains why non-voters receive and store logs without ever contributing to commitment. No contradiction was found in the enclosing paths: the leader lease and election quorum helpers count the same Voter set, and processLogs is bounded by the leader's commitIndex. This is a source-explained negative, so no defect is asserted and the corresponding discriminator is left for execution rather than being inferred from the reading.
limitations: Source-only account: no retained execution yet exercises a mixed Voter/Nonvoter configuration, so the claim rests on reading the producers, not on an observed endpoint.
The reading covers the leader-side commit rule; it does not evaluate non-voter participation in any other mechanism (for example snapshot install or leadership transfer targeting a non-voter).

interpretations.rationale: Comparison: does commit progress track Voter acknowledgements only? Parsed index 2 is the withheld-Nonvoter case: the apply future completed with a nil error, leader_commit went from 3 to 4 and leader_last_index reached 4, while the Nonvoter's own last log index stayed 3, i.e. the entry committed although the Nonvoter never stored it, so nonvoter participation is not needed for commitment. Parsed index 3 is the withheld-Voter case: leader_last_before=4, the leader stored index 5, the Nonvoter stored index 5 as well (nonvoter_has_entry=true), and leader_commit still read 4 when sampled, while the apply future returned 'leadership lost while committing log' rather than success. Read together with the source-derived rule (match set contains only Voter IDs, match() ignores other IDs, recalculate reads only that set), the operands show a stored-and-acknowledged nonvoter entry that did not advance commitIndex. The apply error in case B comes from an independent mechanism - the leader could not contact a quorum of Voters within LeaderLeaseTimeout and stepped down - so case B does not isolate the commit rule by itself; the decisive evidence is the operand contrast between the Nonvoter's stored index and the unchanged commit index, and case A supplies the converse control in the same execution.
limitations: Case B's apply outcome is dominated by lease-driven leadership loss because a single-Voter failure already removes the Voter quorum in a two-Voter cluster, so that case does not alone separate 'commit rule ignores nonvoters' from 'leader stopped being leader'.

Sampling shows commitment had not advanced when polled immediately after the 800ms window; it does not rule out a later advance under a different schedule, though the fact itself is that the nonvoter's stored entry did not by itself advance commitIndex.
Single execution of each case in one process with in-process transports; the withheld-Server scenario assumes a clean transport-level isolation and does not model partial or asymmetric failure.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account of the restart/vote relationship. On startup the node restores currentTerm from the CurrentTerm stable key and the last log entry through setCurrentTerm/setLastLog, and nothing else vote-related is restored, so any same-term duplicate decision must come from the durable keys. In the vote handler the duplicate check reads LastVoteTerm and LastVoteCand from StableStore, returns granted only when the stored candidate bytes equal the requesting candidate, and otherwise returns without setting Granted, so a second different candidate in the same term is denied regardless of restart. persistVote writes the term first and then the candidate before the handler sets Granted, so an acknowledged vote is durable before the response. The older-term rejection is the earlier term comparison, and the restored currentTerm is what makes it effective after a restart. This is a source-explained negative - a protection that defeats an obvious candidate defect - so no defect is asserted and the discriminator is left for execution rather than inferred from reading.
limitations: Source-only: the restart behaviour is read from the constructors and handlers, not yet observed; in particular the claim that a new Raft instance does not consult any other persisted vote artefact rests on reading NewRaft and restoreSnapshot.
The account covers the vote path only; it does not evaluate whether a restart can otherwise reuse stale term or log state in a way that breaks safety (for example a truncated log tail).

interpretations.rationale: Declared predicate: after a restart, a same-term request for the already-voted candidate is still granted while the same-term request for a different candidate is denied, and an older-term request is denied. Parsed index 0 establishes the antecedent producer edge: a real RequestVote granted to candidate A in term 6 left the durable keys at LastVoteTerm=6 and LastVoteCand=A, and the node's term was 6. Parsed index 1 shows the durable vote survived the restart (restored_vote_term=7 with the same candidate A, restored currentTerm 7), but at a term the harness did not choose, because the subject stayed a live member of a real cluster and its peers advanced it past the probe term. Since the restored currentTerm exceeded every post-restart probe term, parsed index 2's three denials are explained by the older-term rule alone: the same-term branch (stored term equal to request term) was never reached, so the comparison's antecedent is unobserved and the predicate is unknown rather than satisfied or violated. The restart-persistence part of the source account is consistent with indices 0 and 1; the same-term-survival part is not yet decided.
limitations: The subject was not isolated: it remained an active voter whose real peers could advance its term, so the post-restart probes were not applicable to the same-term rule and the unknown outcome is a design limitation of this execution, not evidence about the code.

The pre-restart observation shows a grant and the durable keys, but the durable keys were overwritten by the cluster's own later vote at term 7 before the restart, so indices 0 and 1 do not by themselves isolate which request produced the persisted state.

Successor discriminator: isolate the target's transport from its peers (or use a configuration whose other voters are unreachable) before the restart probes, verify the restored currentTerm equals the probe term, and only then compare the same-candidate, other-candidate and older-term grants.

interpretations.rationale: Declared predicate: after a restart, a same-term request for the already-voted candidate is still granted, a same-term request for a different candidate is denied, and an older-term request is denied. Applicability is explicit in the receipt: parsed index 1 reports applicable=true with restored_term=6 and restored_vote_term=6, so the restored currentTerm equals the probe term and the same-term branch is reachable; parsed index 2 reports applicable=true and term_at_probe_end=6, so no election interposed during the probes and all three requests were delivered. Against that base, parsed index 2's operands are: same_cand_granted=true, other_cand_granted=false, older_term_granted=false. The one-candidate-per-term rule is thus preserved across a restart and is read from durable state, consistent with the source account that the handler loads LastVoteTerm/LastVoteCand on every request and that persistVote writes before the grant. This is a protective mechanism, so the account is a refuted suspicion rather than a defect.
limitations: One execution in one process with in-process transports and a rebuilt Raft over the same stores; it does not model a crash before the durable candidate key is written, and the write order (term then candidate) is taken from source rather than exercised.
The isolation used to keep the probe term applicable removes concurrent cluster activity, so the run does not evaluate the same-term branch while other real elections are in flight.
The probes exercise the vote handler through a dedicated transport; they do not exercise a full campaign where the candidate itself counts its own vote.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only account. shouldSnapshot reads the log store's LastIndex and the cached last snapshot index and returns delta >= SnapshotThreshold, with delta computed as an unsigned subtraction. compactLogsWithTrailing deletes everything up to min(snapIdx, lastLogIdx-trailingLogs), and both the snapshot-install path and the user-restore path set the snapshot index to at least the installed index while the log store keeps only newer entries; on a log store that tolerates gaps this can leave LastIndex below the snapshot index, so the subtraction underflows instead of being negative. The account therefore predicts a spurious positive verdict rather than a missed snapshot. I am not asserting a defect: the consequence I can source is limited to an extra snapshot attempt at an unchanged index, and whether that matters depends on consumer expectations for SnapshotThreshold that this snapshot does not settle.
limitations: Source-only: the underflow is derived from reading the arithmetic and the compaction callers, not observed; no retained execution yet shows the emptied-store state.
The consequence is bounded to snapshot scheduling; nothing in this reading shows loss of committed entries or a change to which entries are applied, so it should not be read as a safety claim.

The reachable variant depends on which SnapshotStore and LogStore are in use (monotonic stores remove all logs, gap-tolerant stores compact up to the snapshot), and neither variant has been exercised here.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose committed and applied index already equal its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. Parsed index 0 establishes the control verdict (store_last=4, snapshot_index=0, should_snapshot=false), so the threshold test is discriminating and the large SnapshotThreshold is not saturating the result. Parsed index 1 is the witness: after the production snapshot path ran (Snapshot -> runSnapshots -> takeSnapshot -> compactLogs) the log store was emptied (store_last=0) while the snapshot index was 4 and commit/applied stayed 4, yet shouldSnapshot returned true. Since shouldSnapshot computes delta as an unsigned difference between the store's last index and the snapshot index, the emptied store makes delta underflow rather than go negative, so the verdict becomes true with no new entry. The consequence follows from the same mechanism: runSnapshots calls takeSnapshot whenever shouldSnapshot holds, and takeSnapshot only refuses when the FSM has applied nothing at all, so the node re-creates a snapshot at an unchanged index at each SnapshotInterval. The witness is generated by the target's own compaction after a normal user snapshot, not by stubbing state.
limitations: Scope: the repeating effect requires the FSM's Snapshot to keep succeeding; if Snapshot/Persist errors, the loop reports the error instead and no snapshot is created.

The consequence observed and claimed is limited to redundant snapshot creation and its IO at an unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety violation, and the same index is snapshotted rather than a stale one.

Reached deterministically with TrailingLogs=0 so that compaction trims up to the snapshot index; the install-snapshot and monotonic-store variants that the source reading predicts were not exercised, so the frequency of the state in other configurations is not established.
Single node, one process, in-process transport and InmemStore; the snapshot store is in-memory, so the cost of the redundant snapshots is understated.

interpretations.rationale: Source-only extension. restoreUserSnapshot chooses a last index above both the snapshot and the current log, writes it as the last log and last applied, sets the snapshot to the same index, and then calls removeOldLogs when the log store reports monotonic; removeOldLogs compacts with a trailing count of zero, so a monotonic store ends with no entries while the cached snapshot index is the restored index. shouldSnapshot then compares the store's last index against the snapshot index with unsigned arithmetic, which underflows for that state. This predicts the same verdict as the retained witness but with default TrailingLogs, and it is a distinct producer (restore plus monotonic store) rather than compaction after a caller-configured snapshot. No defect judgment is added here: the existing assertion covers the mechanism, and this question settles only how widely the state is reachable.
limitations: Source-only: the restore-plus-monotonic-store state has not been observed; the claim that a monotonic store ends with an empty log rests on reading removeOldLogs and the caller's compaction contract.

The user-restore path is documented as a disaster-recovery operation that should not be used in normal operation, so reachability through it is a weaker practical case than compaction after an ordinary snapshot.

This question does not re-open the asserted defect or its bounded consequence; it only extends the set of producers, and a negative result would narrow the defect's reachability without changing the mechanism already witnessed.

interpretations.rationale: Promotion of the mechanism witnessed by the retained receipt into durable knowledge, so later interpretations can reuse it without re-reading snapshot.go. The arithmetic and the witness agree: the verdict flips to true in exactly the state where the store's last index is below the cached snapshot index, and the control in the same execution shows the verdict is false when the store still holds entries. No new defect judgment is added and the existing assertion, its bounds and its limitations are unchanged.

Predicate: after a user restore on a monotonic log store with default snapshot configuration, the store's last index falls below the snapshot index and shouldSnapshot therefore reports true, repeating at each SnapshotInterval. Parsed index 1 contradicts it: store_last=105 against snapshot_index=104 with applied index 105 and restore_err nil, so store_emptied is false and should_snapshot is false; parsed index 2 confirms the verdict stays false after several intervals and the snapshot count does not grow. The mechanism that defeats the premise is visible in the sources: removeOldLogs does clear the log store during the restore, but the Restore API then appends a trailng noop entry and waits for it, which puts one log entry above the snapshot index and leaves a small positive delta instead of an underflow. Because the hypothesis is contradicted by the witness, the comparison is violated and this particular producer is refuted; the previously asserted defect stands on its own witness and is not weakened or extended by this result.
limitations: Single execution, one process, in-process transport, in-memory snapshot store and default TrailingLogs/SnapshotThreshold; the restored index was burned 100 above the log, and a restore whose index leaves a different residue was not tried.

The refutation covers the producer reached through Restore() on a monotonic store; it does not speak to the snapshot-install path on a follower, which the source reading also predicts and which remains unexercised.

This result narrows reachability only: the earlier asserted defect and its bounded consequence (redundant snapshot at an unchanged index) were witnessed independently and their limitations now include that the user-restore path is not an additional producer under these conditions.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose committed and applied index already equal its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. The witness stands unchanged: in CheckRun 9cba2e79ff6c4019b0f0381690d9aaab the control sample (store_last=4, snapshot_index=0) gives false, and after the production snapshot path ran the store was emptied (store_last=0) while the snapshot index reached 4 and commit/applied stayed 4, giving true. shouldSnapshot subtracts the store's last index from the snapshot index as unsigned values, so an emptied store underflows instead of going negative; runSnapshots then calls takeSnapshot, which only refuses when nothing at all was applied, so the node recreates a snapshot at the unchanged index each interval. Reachability is now recorded from measurement rather than prediction: CheckRun b78bcab64b0d41b5adaafa98cc0c7f43 shows that a user restore on a monotonic store does not produce the state, because the Restore API appends a trailing noop that leaves store_last=105 above snapshot_index=104, so the verdict stayed false and no additional snapshot was created. The producer that remains demonstrated is compaction after an ordinary snapshot with TrailingLogs=0; the snapshot-install path stays a source-level prediction only.
limitations: The repeating effect requires the FSM's Snapshot to keep succeeding; if Snapshot or Persist errors, the loop reports the error instead and no snapshot is created.

The claimed consequence is limited to redundant snapshot creation and its IO at an unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety violation, and the same index is snapshotted rather than a stale one.

The demonstrated producer uses TrailingLogs=0 so compaction trims up to the snapshot index; with the default trailing count an ordinary snapshot does not empty the store, and the user-restore producer was measured not to empty it either (CheckRun b78bcab64b0d41b5adaafa98cc0c7f43).

The snapshot-install path on a follower, which the source reading predicts can empty the store on a monotonic log store, remains unexercised, so the frequency of the state in that configuration is still unknown.
Single node and one process with in-process transports and an in-memory snapshot store; the cost of the redundant snapshots is understated.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate for this construction: a fresh node that receives an InstallSnapshot ends with its log store below its snapshot index, so shouldSnapshot reports true. Parsed index 1 contradicts it: the install happened (snapshot_index=3, installed_index=3) and the node's log store last index was 5 against that snapshot index, with applied and commit at 5, so store_emptied=false and should_snapshot=false. The reason is visible in the same record: AddVoter appended a configuration entry after the snapshot (leader commit index 4 with snapshot index 3) and replication continued, so the follower's log was repopulated above the installed snapshot index before the sample was taken. The underflow therefore needs the node to be quiescent after the install, which this construction does not provide. The comparison is violated and this route is refuted as constructed; the asserted defect keeps its own witness.
limitations: The sample was taken after catch-up, so it cannot exclude a transient emptied state between the InstallSnapshot and the first following AppendEntries; the observation bounds what persists, not what existed momentarily.

The construction adds the node with AddVoter, which necessarily appends a configuration entry above the snapshot index; a construction that first adds the node, then disconnects it, applies and snapshots on the leader, and finally reconnects would be needed to observe a quiescent install.

One execution, one process, in-process transport, in-memory stores; the leader's TrailingLogs=0 was used to force log-based catch-up to fail, so the leader's own compaction differs from the default configuration.

This narrows reachability only: the earlier asserted defect (redundant snapshot at an unchanged index after a TrailingLogs=0 snapshot) and its bounds are unchanged, and its snapshot-install limitation now records this measured negative.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose applied and commit indices already equal its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. Parsed index 2 contradicts it for a follower that installed a snapshot while its own log store lagged: snapshot_index=8 and applied_index=8 with store_last=5, store_emptied=true, should_snapshot=true, and no new entry in this node's own store above the snapshot. Combined with parsed index 1, the producing sequence is the leader compacting its log and the follower needing a snapshot: the follower's install succeeds at index 8, but the compaction that follows the install respects the trailing-log count, so the follower's older entries below index 8 are not removed and the store's last index stays below the snapshot index. shouldSnapshot then subtracts the two as unsigned values, underflows, and reports true, so runSnapshots schedules a snapshot at the unchanged index on every interval until the follower's log grows past the snapshot index. The same witness pattern as the earlier TrailingLogs=0 run therefore also occurs with default follower settings during ordinary catch-up.
limitations: The repeating effect still requires the FSM's Snapshot to keep succeeding; if Snapshot or Persist errors, the loop reports the error and no snapshot is created.

The claimed consequence stays bounded to redundant snapshot creation and its IO at an unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety effect, and the snapshot taken is at the correct (unchanged) index.

The construction forced log-based catch-up to fail by compacting the leader's log (TrailingLogs=0 on the leader), so the leader's configuration differs from the defaults even though the measured follower's did not.

The emptied-below-snapshot condition is met while the follower holds stale entries below the snapshot index rather than by an entirely empty store; the underflow follows from the comparison, not from emptiness as such.

Single execution, one process, in-process transports and in-memory stores; the cost of the redundant snapshots is understated, and how long the condition persists depends on how quickly the follower's log advances.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose applied index already equals its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot, and if it does the trigger must not create another snapshot at that unchanged index. Parsed index 0 contradicts the first half: store_last=0 against snapshot_index=3 with applied_index=3 and should_snapshot=true. Parsed indices 1 and 2 contradict the second: two production takeSnapshot calls each returned a stored snapshot id with err nil and raised the stored-snapshot count 1 to 2 to 3 while snapshot_index and applied_index stayed at 3, so the node keeps doing redundant snapshot work at the index it already covered. Read with the earlier witnesses, the producing condition is a store index below the snapshot index (emptied by compaction or left behind by an installed snapshot), and the effect is repeated snapshot creation and its IO, not a wrong decision about which entries are committed or applied. Parsed index 1 also shows the InmemStore reporting a wrapped store_last after the compaction inside takeSnapshot, which is a store implementation artifact recorded separately rather than evidence for the trigger's arithmetic.
limitations: The observed repetition used direct takeSnapshot calls instead of waiting on SnapshotInterval, so the cadence in wall-clock terms is still not measured; what is established is that every trigger does the redundant work while the condition holds.
The claim remains bounded to redundant snapshot creation and its IO at the unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety effect.

The wrapped store_last=18446744073709551615 in parsed indices 1 and 2 comes from the in-memory log store's delete-range bookkeeping after repeated compaction, so that specific value should not be attributed to other log stores; the generic reading is the emptied-store sample in parsed index 0.
Single node, one process, in-process transports and an in-memory snapshot store, so the real cost of the redundant snapshots is understated.
The condition persists only while the node's log stays below its snapshot index; a node that receives new entries above the snapshot index stops reporting the spurious verdict.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose applied index already equals its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. Parsed index 0 contradicts it (store_last=0 against snapshot_index=3 with applied_index=3 and should_snapshot=true), and that verdict persisted in every later sample. The consequence is now measured rather than assumed: the node's own snapshot loop created snapshots at the unchanged index 3 while the applied index stayed at 3 (count 1 to 2 to 3 across parsed indices 1 and 2, i.e. within about 400ms at a 100ms interval), and then the stored count remained at 3 for the remaining four samples out to 1209ms even though should_snapshot stayed true. Two readings are consistent with the plateau and this run does not separate them: the loop may be attempting snapshots that are not being stored, or the attempts are no longer being made, and the harness recorded neither runSnapshots' logged errors nor an attempt counter. What the receipt supports is therefore: the spurious verdict is persistent while the store index stays below the snapshot index, and it does cause redundant snapshot creation at an unchanged index, observed twice. It does not support a per-interval recurrence, and I withdraw that phrasing. The defect assertion itself rests on the persistent spurious verdict with redundant work, and that stands.
limitations: The recurrence rate is not established: the observed count stopped growing after two additions even though the verdict stayed true, and the run did not record snapshot attempts or runSnapshots' logged errors, so whether attempts continued without being stored is unknown.
The claim remains bounded to redundant snapshot work at an unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety effect.

The wrapped store_last=18446744073709551615 seen from parsed index 1 onward comes from the in-memory log store's delete-range bookkeeping after repeated compaction and should not be attributed to other log stores; the generic reading is the emptied-store sample in parsed index 0.
The interval was set to 100ms for observation, which is far shorter than any production default, so the observed timing is not a production cadence.
Single node, one process, in-process transports and an in-memory snapshot store, so the real cost of the redundant snapshots is understated.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose applied index already equals its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. Parsed index 0 contradicts it (store_last=0 against snapshot_index=3 with applied_index=3 and should_snapshot=true) and the verdict held in every later sample of the same execution. The consequence is measured but bounded: the node's own loop created snapshots at the unchanged index 3 twice within about 400ms while the applied index stayed fixed at 3 (parsed indices 1 and 2), and the stored count then stayed at 3 through the end of the window (parsed index 6) although the verdict remained true. A search of the same receipt's stdout for the node's snapshot-failure messages returned none, so the later samples were not accompanied by reported snapshot failures; the remaining explanations are that the loop was not scheduled in that window or that successful attempts did not change the stored count, and this receipt does not separate them. What the evidence supports is the persistent spurious verdict with redundant snapshot work at an unchanged index; a per-interval recurrence is not supported and that wording is withdrawn.
limitations: The recurrence rate is not established: the stored count stopped growing after two additions while the verdict stayed true, and the receipt contains no snapshot-failure logs, so whether attempts continued, and whether any succeeded without changing the stored count, is unknown from this execution.
The claim remains bounded to redundant snapshot work at an unchanged index; nothing here shows loss of committed entries, a change to which entries are applied, or any safety effect.

interpretations.rationale: Predicate: a node whose applied index already equals its snapshot index must not report that it should snapshot. Parsed index 0 of CheckRun a4a0cbfa094b4d1982032d9de0652861 contradicts it (store_last=0 against snapshot_index=3 with applied_index=3 and should_snapshot=true) and the verdict held through every later sample of that run, so the spurious trigger is established independently of any timing question. The consequence is witnessed as snapshot creation at the unchanged index while the applied index stayed at 3: the stored count moved 1 to 2 to 3 across parsed indices 1 and 2, which requires at least two successful creations. Reading the in-memory snapshot store shows why that count then flattened: Create replaces the single latest snapshot and List returns only that one, so the stored count cannot be used as an attempt counter, and the file-backed store used by the cluster helper reaps older snapshots per its retain count. The flat tail therefore does not show that the loop stopped; it shows my proxy stopped measuring, and I withdraw both the per-interval wording and any inference from the flat tail. The claim stands on the persistent spurious verdict plus the redundant creation actually witnessed, with cadence left unmeasured.
limitations: Cadence remains unmeasured: stored-snapshot counts cannot serve as an attempt counter for these stores, so any rate claim needs an attempt-level observation such as the FSM's Snapshot calls.
